historical_timeline.summary: Aversions, counting, calculating, and acts in multiples of three, as he later described them.
Vivid images with flashes of light; first banishes an image by effort.
Cholera at seventeen; from about this age he visualizes inventions in detail.
Moves to Budapest; complete breakdown of the nerves.
Wardenclyffe tower and laboratory under construction.
Later years: pigeons, heightened germ aversion, compulsive handwashing.
Dies alone in the New Yorker Hotel.

claims.statement: Nikola Tesla was born on 10 July 1856 in the village of Smiljan, in what is now Croatia, to Serbian parents; his father was an Orthodox priest.
claims.clinical_interpretation: PBS describes him as born a subject of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

claims.statement: In his memoir My Inventions (1919) he wrote that in boyhood he suffered from "a peculiar affliction due to the appearance of images, often accompanied by strong flashes of light", pictures of things he had really seen, which caused him great discomfort and anxiety; at about twelve he first banished an image by wilful effort, but he never controlled the flashes, which grew stronger until he was about twenty-five.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own retrospective account; the phenomena have been read in different ways (CLM-0013).

claims.statement: He wrote that he had a violent aversion to women's earrings, that the sight of a pearl would almost give him a fit, and that he would not touch the hair of other people; in 1919 he wrote that he was still "not insensible to some of these upsetting impulses".

He wrote that he counted the steps in his walks and calculated the cubical contents of soup plates, coffee cups, and pieces of food, or his meal was unenjoyable, and that all repeated acts had to be divisible by three, and if he missed he felt impelled to do it all over again, even if it took hours.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account. Counting and arithmetic rituals of this kind are now recognized as compulsions, but that reading is retrospective (CLM-0013, CLM-0014).

claims.statement: He wrote that from about seventeen he could visualize his inventions with the greatest facility and needed no models, drawings, or experiments.

In 1881 he moved to Budapest to help install a telephone exchange; there, in his own account, he suffered "the complete breakdown of the nerves", with extreme sensitivity to sound, light, and vibration, a pulse he described as ranging up to 260 beats, and twitching and tremors; a physician called his illness unique and incurable, and he recovered with a powerful desire to live and the help of a friend.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own retrospective account of a severe illness; no diagnosis can be made from it.

claims.statement: In 1884 he went to New York; by 1901 he was building a tower and laboratory for wireless transmission at Wardenclyffe on Long Island.
He claimed that his working hours at his first job in New York were from 10:30 in the morning until 5 the next morning, and even into old age he said he slept only two or three hours a night.
After the Wardenclyffe project was abandoned for lack of money in 1905, PBS reports, he had a complete nervous breakdown.

In later years he rescued injured pigeons and nursed them in his hotel room; his aversion to germs heightened, and he began to wash his hands compulsively and would eat only boiled foods, which prompted speculation about his mental well-being.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Later-life behaviors as reported; not a diagnosis.

claims.statement: Financial difficulties continued as his patents expired; increasingly reclusive, he lived alone in a room in the New Yorker Hotel until he died there on 7 January 1943.
A 2013 neurology review reads the experiences he described in his autobiography as including migraine auras, synesthesias, obsessions, and compulsions.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective interpretation; only the abstract was read.

claims.statement: The roster lists obsessive-compulsive disorder and probable autism spectrum features; no diagnosis was made in his lifetime, a diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive disorder is a later interpretation of his own accounts, and autism is speculative and is not diagnosed in this record.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Assess and treat severe obsessive-compulsive disorder in a 45-year-old electrical engineer, following the APA practice guideline (2007, with the 2013 guideline watch) and NICE CG31: a structured assessment with the Y-BOCS symptom checklist and severity scale, screening for depression, anxiety, tics, bipolar disorder, psychosis, and substance use, exposure and response prevention as first-line psychotherapy, sertraline raised in 50 mg steps to an effective dose, with the longer trial OCD needs, the effect of the rituals on his work, meals, sleep, and hands, an examination that respects his contamination fears without forcing exposures, and a structured suicide-risk assessment with a safety plan and the 988 Lifeline, while treating his historical rituals as his own accounts and not mocking or sensationalizing them.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Tesla returns two weeks after starting sertraline 50 mg each morning. He had mild nausea for four days and looser stools, now settled, and no headache, restlessness, or change in sleep. He has missed no doses. He has had his first session of exposure and response prevention and began building his list of feared situations. He still washes his hands about 50 times a day, but uses the ointment after each wash and the cracks are less painful. He has eaten two meals a day most days. He has had no suicidal thoughts. He saw Dr. Feinberg-Osei of psychiatry this morning.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Tesla returns six weeks after starting sertraline 50 mg. He has had no side effects since the first week and has missed no doses. He has had five ERP sessions and has practiced touching door handles without washing for ten minutes, and eating lunch without calculating its volume on two days a week. He washes about 30 times a day. Counting his steps is still hard to resist, and repeating laboratory steps in threes still costs him about two hours a day. He saw the dietitian and now eats three meals on most days. He sleeps about five hours. He has had no suicidal thoughts.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Tesla is a 46-year-old electrical engineer in treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder with exposure and response prevention and sertraline 150 mg, who asked for a same-day visit. Thirty-six hours ago he began vomiting, followed by watery diarrhea about six times a day, cramping, and aching. Two engineers on his staff had the same illness last week. He vomited four times yesterday and not since this morning, and he is keeping down small sips of water. He has had no blood in the stool, severe abdominal pain, or high fever. He vomited his sertraline yesterday morning and has not taken it since. The illness has stirred his contamination fears: he has been washing his hands more than he has for months and has wiped down his apartment twice. He is upset that this undoes his progress. He has had no suicidal thoughts.

referral.question: Severe obsessive-compulsive symptoms (Y-BOCS 28) with good insight in a 45-year-old electrical engineer, with weight loss from food rituals and hand dermatitis from washing. Please confirm the diagnosis, review comorbidity, and advise on sertraline dosing, the length of the trial, and what to do if the response is partial
referral.urgency: Soon, within two weeks; no current suicidal ideation
referral.pertinent_history: For many years, and worse over the past six months as his company's largest project has come under pressure, he has had intrusive fears of dirt and germs and a need for numbers to come out right. He washes his hands 40 to 60 times a day, until they crack; wipes cutlery before eating; avoids handshakes; counts his steps; repeats actions until they are done in threes; and calculates the volume of each portion of food before he can eat it, so meals take up to an hour and he often skips them. Rituals take three to four hours a day. He recognizes the thoughts as excessive. He has lost about 4 kg in six months (63.8 kg, BMI 18.1) and sleeps about four hours a night. He describes vivid deliberate visual imagery of his designs, which he knows is his own imagination. Y-BOCS 28; PHQ-9 8 with item 9 scored 0; GAD-7 12; AUDIT-C 1. Metabolic panel, TSH, and hemoglobin normal; albumin 3.8 g/dL and vitamin B12 284 pg/mL, both low-normal. No suicidal ideation, intent, plan, or past self-harm; no firearms; a safety plan with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline was made today. He starts sertraline 50 mg today and weekly exposure and response prevention with the clinic psychologist, with petrolatum for his hands and a dietitian visit
questions: Do you confirm obsessive-compulsive disorder, and is there a tic disorder, bipolar disorder, psychosis, obsessive-compulsive personality disorder, or an eating disorder to consider?
When and how fast should sertraline be raised, to what dose, and how long should the trial last before we judge it?
Is exposure and response prevention alone or combined with sertraline right for him?
What should we do if the response is partial at the maximum dose?
How should we handle his food rituals and weight loss, and his contamination fears during examinations?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Tesla is seen at the request of Dr. Kovač-Holt, two weeks after starting sertraline 50 mg, which he tolerates with brief nausea. He describes contamination, symmetry, and number obsessions since childhood that have waxed and waned and worsened over the past six months under work pressure, with washing, counting, repeating, and calculating compulsions that take three to four hours a day. He resists them at a cost of rising anxiety and recognizes them as excessive. He has no motor or vocal tics, no period of elevated mood or reduced need for sleep with racing thoughts beyond his long-standing short sleep, no hallucinations or fixed false beliefs, no hoarding, and no concern about his appearance. His vivid imagery of designs is voluntary and recognized as his own. His perfectionism is confined to the rituals he finds distressing and does not otherwise rule his relationships. He does not fear weight gain or dislike his body shape; he skips meals because calculating them is exhausting. He has never harmed himself and has no suicidal thoughts. He drinks rarely and uses no drugs

The restricted eating is driven by the calculating ritual, not by fear of weight gain or of choking, so it is treated within the OCD plan rather than as a separate eating disorder.
